Section 1: Executive Summary & Recent Operational Reality

1.1 Executive Commentary & Management Strategy (Q1 2026)

Following the strategic leadership transition in March 2026—where long-time CFO Mateus Scherer stepped up as Chief Executive Officer and Treasury Officer Diego Salgado assumed the CFO and Investor Relations role—StoneCo (STNE) delivered a steady Q1 2026 report. Total Revenue and Income from continuing operations reached BRL 3.58 billion (+6.5% YoY), while Adjusted Net Income came in at BRL 549 million (+3.5% YoY). Adjusted Basic EPS grew at a significantly faster rate of 15% YoY to BRL 2.19, directly driven by persistent share repurchases.

CEO Mateus Scherer characterized Q1 2026 as a transitional period shaped by three major operating forces:

  • Macroeconomic Pressure on Micro/SMBs: Persistent elevated interest rates in Brazil continue to weigh heavily on smaller merchants. Non-performing loans (NPLs) ran above management’s baseline expectations, forcing a step-up in credit loss provisions that contracted Adjusted Gross Profit Margin from 44.4% to 41.6% YoY.
  • Client Cohort Churn & Base Rationalization: Elevated customer churn occurred among lower-margin clients onboarded during 2025. Management actively purged lower-engagement micro-merchants to focus resources on higher-value SMBs, resulting in a 5% sequential decline in active clients to 4.7 million.
  • Rail Shift (PIX vs. Credit Cards): Brazil’s central bank instant payment system (PIX) continues to capture payment volume. PIX QR Code volume outpaced traditional card Total Payment Volume (TPV). While PIX carries lower immediate take rates than credit card receivables anticipation, it deepens daily engagement and acts as a funnel for high-margin banking deposits.

2H26 Operational Re-Acceleration Plan: Management signaled that the softer first half of 2026 will give way to operational re-acceleration in 2H26. Strategy centers on recalibrating credit underwriting models, expanding collateralized secured credit products (credit cards backed by daily receivables capture and asset-backed loans), lowering cohort churn, and simplifying product onboarding.

1.2 Corporate Announcements & Capital Allocation Playbook

StoneCo’s capital allocation has undergone a dramatic shift, transitioning proceeds from non-core asset sales into direct shareholder cash distributions:

  • Linx Divestiture: StoneCo completed the sale of its retail software unit, Linx, closing the transaction in early 2026. The strategic divestiture allows management to shed software execution friction and refocus resources entirely on core merchant acquiring, business banking, and credit solutions.
  • Extraordinary Dividend ($2.53 / Share): Leveraging proceeds from the Linx closing, the Board declared a one-off extraordinary cash dividend of $2.53 per share (totaling approximately BRL 3.08 billion), which was paid out on May 4, 2026. Management explicitly reiterated that this is a non-recurring event tied directly to asset monetization and does not constitute a formal recurring dividend policy.
  • Aggressive Share Buyback Execution: Year-to-date capital returns totaled BRL 3.6 billion (representing a distribution yield of roughly 27% including the Linx proceeds). Management has committed at least BRL 1.4 billion in additional capital for share repurchases through the end of fiscal 2026 under its existing buyback authorization.

Section 2: Business Model & Competitive Moat

2.1 Unit Economics & Operational Metrics Reality

Evaluating StoneCo’s core engine reveals a shift toward monetization per merchant through banking and credit, even as payment volume growth moderates:

Competitive Landscape Dynamics

  • vs. PagSeguro (PagBank): PagSeguro remains StoneCo’s primary fintech competitor in the long-tail micro-merchant and SMB market. While PagSeguro has leaned into consumer/merchant digital banking scale, StoneCo maintains higher average TPV per SMB merchant and stronger localized field distribution. Both players face yield compression in raw processing fees, forcing a push into banking deposits and working capital loans.
  • vs. Cielo & Rede (Itaú Unibanco): Legacy bank acquirers (Cielo and Itaú's Rede) control large enterprise flow but continue to lose ground in middle-market SMBs. Rede and Cielo aggressively bundle bank credit lines and offer low receivables anticipation rates, forcing StoneCo to continuously prove the value of its software-like service model and proprietary POS technology.

2.2 Economic Moat & Ecosystem Lock-In

StoneCo’s competitive advantage does not stem from pure payment processing—which has largely become a commoditized utility in Brazil—but rather from a localized distribution engine and product bundling:

1. Proprietary "Stone Hub" Distribution Model:

Unlike pure-play digital acquirers or traditional bank branches, StoneCo operates an in-house network of over 500 localized "Hubs" across secondary and tertiary Brazilian cities. These Hubs house hyper-local sales teams, technical support staff, and logistics operatives capable of delivering, installing, or swapping terminal hardware within hours. This high-touch, physical proximity builds deep trust with non-tech-native local business owners, serving as a primary defense against digital-only competitors like PagSeguro or Mercado Pago.

2. Switching Costs & Financial Ecosystem Lock-In:

StoneCo successfully transitions merchants from single-product card acquirers into full financial ecosystem clients. Strategic integration includes:

  • Automated Receivables Settlement: Merchants process POS card sales directly into their StoneCo business bank accounts (BRL 10.1B in deposits).
  • Collateralized Working Capital Credit: Credit products (BRL 3.2B portfolio) are structured so loan principal repayments are automatically intercepted from daily card sales receivables before cash hits the merchant's account. This reduces credit defaults and creates high operational friction if a merchant attempts to churn to a competing acquirer.

3. Stock-Based Compensation (SBC) & Shareholder Dilution Discipline:

In assessing long-term shareholder value, SBC is treated as a real operational cash expense that dilutes ownership. To offset executive equity incentives, StoneCo’s capital allocation strategy actively utilizes share repurchases. Over 29 million shares were repurchased through late 2025, and with BRL 1.4+ billion remaining under current authorization, net share count reduction has allowed EPS to outpace net income growth (+15% EPS vs +3.5% Net Income in Q1 2026).

Section 3: Real Cash Flow, SBC & Capital Structure Audit

As the Cash Flow, Stock-Based Compensation (SBC) Dilution, and Balance Sheet Auditor for StoneCo Ltd. (NASDAQ: STNE), this audit examines the company's financial releases, Form 20-F annual filings, and Form 6-K earnings statements. The objective is to strip away non-GAAP management adjustments, treat equity grants as true economic expenses, and evaluate the financial risk profile stemming from credit expansion in a high-interest Brazilian macroeconomic environment (Selic at 14%).

1. True Cash Generation & SBC Dilution Audit

Management’s reported "Adjusted Net Income" routinely adds back Stock-Based Compensation (SBC) as an unencumbered non-cash item. In institutional equity analysis, SBC represents direct economic dilution to existing shareholders and a future cash drain via share repurchases required to sterilize bracket expansion.

  • SBC Treatment as a Real Operating Cost: In Q1 2026, StoneCo reported SBC expenses of approximately US$21.1 million (R$110 million+). When deducting SBC as a real operational expense, StoneCo's reported Adjusted Net Income of R$549.1 million contracts to a True Cash Net Income of approximately R$439 million—a ~20% haircut to headline profitability.
  • LTIP Pool Expansion Dilution: Concurrently with the US$2.53/share extraordinary dividend announcement, the Board approved an additional 3.8 million shares for the Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP) pool. This dilutive expansion offsets a notable portion of share count reductions achieved via ordinary buybacks.
  • Operating Cash Flow Adjustments: While reported operating cash flows appear robust due to non-cash credit loss provision add-backs, true cash generation from core payments is increasingly consumed by working capital requirements to fund loan originations and rising debt servicing obligations.

2. Capital Allocation & Share Buyback Execution

StoneCo’s capital allocation strategy in early 2026 was defined by the monetization of non-core assets, specifically the closing of the Linx divestment in February 2026.

  • Linx Sale & Extraordinary Dividend: The divestment enabled a US$2.53 per share extraordinary cash dividend paid on May 4, 2026, totaling ~R$3.08 billion (US$600M+). While providing an immediate ~27% distribution yield YTD, this is a one-time liquidity event derived from asset sales, not sustainable operating cash flows.
  • Total Shareholder Return (YTD): Total capital returned to shareholders YTD reaches R$3.6 billion, combining the R$3.08B special dividend with ~R$0.52B–R$0.60B in ordinary open-market share buybacks (repurchasing over 20M shares between Jan–Jun 2026 at an average price of ~$10.50–$14.50).
  • Remaining Buyback Capacity: StoneCo retains a R$1.4 billion buyback commitment for the remainder of 2026. However, repurchases must be balanced against cash reserves required to buffer rising credit defaults.

  • Ordinary Share Buybacks Executed: R$0.60 Billion
  • Total Capital Returned YTD: R$3.60 Billion
  • Remaining Authorized Share Buybacks (FY2026): R$1.40 Billion

3. Credit Portfolio Expansion, NPL Spikes & Balance Sheet Vulnerabilities

The primary fundamental risk facing StoneCo is its strategic shift from a pure-play merchant acquiring/payments network into a credit provider. As payments growth moderates, StoneCo has leveraged its balance sheet to drive total revenue growth via working capital loans to SMBs.

  • Credit Portfolio Acceleration: The working capital loan book surged 122.5% YoY to R$3.22 billion in Q1 2026 (up 14%–25% sequentially), generating R$297 million in direct credit revenue (+186% YoY).
  • Severe Credit Quality Deterioration: Non-Performing Loans (>90-day NPL ratio) spiked to 6.98% (approaching 7.0%), while the Cost of Risk (CoR) exploded to 21.9%. Credit provisions expanded over 50% QoQ, directly driving gross margin compression from 44.4% down to 41.6%.
  • Macro Stress (High Selic Rate): Brazil's benchmark Selic interest rate lingering around 14% creates a dual headwind: it raises funding costs for merchant receivables and increases default velocity among SMB borrowers. Management acknowledged that full-year 2026 Adjusted Gross Profit will track toward the bottom end of its guidance range (R$6.6B–R$7.0B).
  • Adjusted Net Cash Position: Post-Linx sale and post-extraordinary dividend distribution, StoneCo’s adjusted net cash position stands at R$4.94 billion. While liquidity remains healthy, the cash cushion is increasingly locked up as capital reserves to backstop credit impairments.

Auditor Conclusion & Governance Warning:

While StoneCo's return of R$3.6B to shareholders via the Linx proceeds provides short-term cash yield, the core underlying business model is migrating toward higher risk. Deducting SBC lowers true earnings by 20%, and expanding credit origination into a 14% Selic rate environment is driving Cost of Risk to unsustainable levels (21.9%). Capital allocation must pivot from aggressively consuming cash on buybacks toward fortifying provision coverage if NPLs exceed 7.0%.

Section 4: Institutional Ownership & Catalyst Tracking

A rigorous examination of official SEC filings (Form 20-F, Form 6-K) and recent 13F disclosures reveals a shifting, highly concentrated institutional ownership structure for StoneCo Ltd. (STNE). Despite historical price volatility and macro headwinds in Brazil, institutional whales retain substantial control over the equity float.

1. 13F Institutional Whale Tracking & Ownership Structure

Institutional ownership stands at over 80% of total float, representing roughly 192.6 million shares held across 500+ reporting institutions. The top 10 institutional holders command over 56% of total disclosed institutional shares.

  • Key Institutional Holders: Dominant positions are anchored by tier-1 asset managers including BlackRock, Inc., Madrone Advisors, LLC, FMR LLC (Fidelity), and State Street Corp, alongside leading Latin American specialized long-only and hedge funds such as SPX Equities Gestão de Recursos and Squadra Investments.
  • Berkshire Hathaway Legacy Status: It is critical to confirm that Berkshire Hathaway, which famously backed StoneCo at its 2018 IPO at $24.00/share, has fully exited its position. The stock's current trading range ($9.50–$11.50) represents a >55% discount to Berkshire's entry cost, creating an asymmetric setup where fundamental value far decoupled from historical institutional cost bases.

2. Executive Insider Activity & Management Continuity

Insider buying provides a high-conviction signal of fundamental undervaluation, particularly following executive leadership changes:

  • CFO Insider Open-Market Purchase: In May 2026, newly appointed Chief Financial Officer & IR Officer Diego Salgado executed an open-market purchase of 22,490 Class A shares at an average price of $9.66 per share (total outlay ~$217,000). This direct commitment occurred near STNE's 52-week low ($9.45), serving as a clear vote of confidence from the executive leading treasury and capital deployment.
  • Leadership Transition: The appointment of Mateus Scherer Schwening as CEO (succeeding Pedro Zinner, who stepped up as Chairman of the Board) preserves strategic continuity. Scherer previously spearheaded StoneCo's credit re-architecting and banking expansion, ensuring capital allocation remains anchored on ROIC and cash distribution.

3. Key Near-Term & Strategic Catalysts

StoneCo's thesis is supported by several major operational and corporate catalysts over the next 12 to 24 months:

  • Linx Divestiture & Capital Return Blitz: Following the closing of the Linx software unit sale to TOTVS for ~BRL 3.1 billion, management authorized and executed an extraordinary distribution of BRL 3.08 billion (~$2.53/share) in April/May 2026. Combined with ongoing share buybacks, year-to-date capital returned to shareholders reached BRL 3.6 billion (~27% distribution yield).
  • Committed Share Repurchase Execution: At least BRL 1.4 billion remains explicitly committed for additional share buybacks through year-end 2026. At single-digit P/E multiples (P/E ~5.5x–6.0x), this buyback yield (>10.5% annualized) provides compounding EPS accretion.
  • Funding Cost Optimization: CFO Diego Salgado confirmed that StoneCo reduced its overall cost of funding from 100% of the benchmark CDI rate down to ~87% of CDI through retail deposit expansion (reaching over BRL 10.1 billion in deposits). In a high SELIC environment (~10.5%–11.25%), every 100 bps reduction in funding costs yields massive net interest margin (NIM) expansion.
  • Controlled Credit Portfolio Scaling: Re-accelerating the working capital and merchant credit portfolio to BRL 3.2 billion (+14% QoQ) while enforcing tight loss underwriting models.

Section 5: Ballpark Valuation & Key Invalidation Triggers

To establish a down-to-earth valuation for StoneCo Ltd., we employ a localized 3-year scenario matrix (2026–2028). The model explicitly incorporates Brazilian sovereign risk parameters, management guidance targets, and disciplined capital allocation assumptions.

1. Macro Framework & Localized Discount Parameters

  • Sovereign Benchmark & Discount Rate (Cost of Equity): With Brazil's SELIC benchmark interest rate maintained at ~10.50%–11.25%, the localized equity discount rate (Cost of Equity) is set at 14.0% – 16.0%. This captures Brazil's sovereign yield spread, currency risk premium, and equity beta.
  • Exchange Rate Baseline: Valuations utilize a baseline currency conversion rate of USD/BRL ~5.50.
  • Management Guidance Anchors:
    • 2026 Adjusted EPS Guidance: BRL 10.80 – BRL 11.40 (Midpoint: BRL 11.10).
    • 2027 Adjusted EPS Guidance: BRL 11.80 – BRL 13.40 (Midpoint: BRL 12.60).

3. Invalidation & Falsification Framework

To prevent thesis drift, the investment case for STNE is strictly bound to five hard falsification metrics. If any of the following triggers occur, the long fundamental thesis is broken:

  1. Credit Risk Overextension / NPL Blowout:
    Trigger: Cost of Risk (provision expenses relative to total credit portfolio) exceeding 25% of gross credit revenues, or NPL 90+ ratios surging above 10.0%.
    Rationale: Indicates a breakdown in underwriting algorithms, repeating the disastrous 2021 non-performing loan crisis that severely impaired equity value.
  2. Guidance Failure (2026 EPS Floor Breach):
    Trigger: Full-year 2026 Adjusted EPS falling below BRL 10.00 (breaching the bottom end of management's BRL 10.80–11.40 range).
    Rationale: Signal that margin contraction and client churn outweigh share buyback benefits.
  3. Core SMB Payment Hub Market Share Erosion:
    Trigger: Total active SMB client count dropping below 4.2 million (from 4.7M in Q1 2026), or double-digit annual TPV loss in core micro/SMB hubs to key competitors (PagBank, Mercado Pago, Rede).
    Rationale: StoneCo's banking and credit cross-sell thesis relies entirely on maintaining the primary payment acquiring relationship with merchants. Loss of acquiring share destroys the distribution engine.
  4. Capital Allocation Derailment:
    Trigger: Management failing to complete the committed BRL 1.4B+ buyback plan by year-end 2026, or shifting capital toward speculative, dilutive cross-border M&A rather than returning free cash flow.
    Rationale: At P/E multiples near 5.6x, repurchasing shares is the highest-ROIC allocation available. Abandoning buybacks destroys the margin of safety.
  5. Regulatory & Macro Structural Shocks:
    Trigger: Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) imposing artificial caps on credit card pre-payment / interchange fees, or total funding cost rising back above 95% of CDI.
    Rationale: Directly compresses Net Interest Income (NII) and eliminates StoneCo's competitive advantage in merchant working capital financing.
